before.title: 1.8L BP head gasket failure and cooling-system age wear
before.description: The 1.8L BP (and the smaller 1.5L/1.6L) can develop head-gasket failure as they accumulate miles, often triggered or accelerated by an aging cooling system - a stuck thermostat, tired radiator, failed fan motor, or slow coolant loss leading to an overheat event. Signs are overheating on longer drives, coolant disappearing with bubbling/back-pressure in the reservoir or radiator, white anti-freeze-smelling exhaust smoke, and oil turning a tan 'coffee-with-too-much-creamer' color when coolant mixes in. Left unaddressed it warps the aluminum head.
before.solution: Confirm with a combustion-gas (block) test or compression/leak-down test. Repair means removing the head, sending it to a machine shop for crack/dye testing and resurfacing, and reassembling with a quality (Fel-Pro or OEM) head gasket and new head bolts to the factory torque sequence. Refresh the cooling system at the same time - thermostat, coolant, water pump, and inspect the radiator - to prevent a repeat.
symptoms: coolant loss with bubbling in reservoir/radiator

before.title: Alternator Premature Failure and Charging Issues
before.description: Proteges experience premature alternator failure, often between 80,000-120,000 miles. The voltage regulator and brush assembly wear out, causing undercharging (battery dies) or overcharging (bulbs blow, battery boils). The alternator is mounted low on the engine where it is exposed to heat and road spray. Remanufactured units often have short lifespans as well.
before.solution: Replace the alternator with a new (not remanufactured) unit if possible ($200-$350). If budget is tight, a reman from DENSO or Bosch is better than generic brands. The replacement is 1-2 hours labor. Replace the serpentine belt at the same time. Test output voltage at the battery (should be 13.8-14.4V) and load test the battery, which may have been damaged by the failing alternator.

communityRecommendations.content: Spend the extra $50 and get a new DENSO alternator instead of a reman. The reman alternators for the Protege have terrible quality — I went through 3 remans in 2 years before buying a new Denso that's lasted 5 years.

before.title: Automatic transaxle erratic/harsh shifting and complete failures
before.description: The 4-speed automatic in 1995-1998 Proteges is a common weak point. Owners report harsh downshifts when lifting off the throttle, jerking, unexpected lurching between reverse and drive, flaring, and eventual complete failure (friction material disintegrating and circulating as debris). A frequent electrical-side cause is the valve-body internal wiring harness (transaxle fluid temperature sensor circuit) being pinched by a metal retaining clip, producing erratic shifts, MIL on, and a flashing O/D OFF indicator light - addressed by Mazda TSB 01098 (Oct 1998). CarComplaints ranks the 1995 model year as the most complained-about Protege, with transmission among the top categories.
before.solution: Start with a diagnostic and pan drop: for flashing O/D light and erratic shifts, inspect/repair the pinched valve-body harness per TSB 01098 before condemning the unit; also check the neutral safety/range switch, another common cause of a blinking O/D light. Service the fluid and filter. If friction material has already contaminated the transaxle (slipping, no drive, metal in fluid), a rebuild or replacement is required.

before.title: Distributor failure causing intermittent stalling and hot no-start
before.description: First-generation Proteges (and 1.5L/1.6L second-gen cars) use a camshaft-driven distributor that houses the ignition pickup. With age these distributors suffer internal bearing wear and moisture intrusion past the seal, which corrodes the pickup and shaft. The result is a car that runs fine cold but stalls once hot and refuses to restart until it cools, or a sudden loss of spark and a crank-no-start. Documented cases include a 1990 Protege that ran ~10 minutes then abruptly stalled until cold (fixed by a dealer distributor replacement) and a 1.8L DOHC no-start where new coil, wires, cap and rotor did not cure it until the distributor was replaced.
before.solution: Confirm loss of spark, then replace the complete distributor assembly (the internal pickup/bearing is not reliably serviceable on a worn unit). Reinstall carefully - the rotor can seat in more than one position, so mark distributor-to-block orientation and rotor direction before removal to preserve base timing. Replace cap, rotor, wires and check the seal while in there.

before.title: EGR insufficient-flow code (P0401) with rough idle / check-engine light
before.description: OBD-II Proteges (1996-1998) of this era commonly set P0401 (EGR flow insufficient) as they age. The carbon-clogged EGR valve and passages are the classic cause, but on these cars the fault is frequently the EGR boost sensor (a firewall-mounted MAP-type sensor whose vacuum nipple/line clogs with carbon) or a cracked/leaking vacuum line feeding it rather than the valve itself. Symptoms are an illuminated check-engine light, rough or unstable idle, and occasional light hesitation. Because it is an emissions monitor, it will also cause emissions-test failures.
before.solution: Read codes to confirm P0401 (and rule out related lean/misfire codes). Remove and clean the EGR valve and its intake passages of carbon; inspect the EGR boost sensor and every vacuum line to it for cracks, carbon-clogging, or disconnection and replace as needed. Replace the EGR valve only if it is confirmed stuck or leaking after the cheaper sensor/vacuum checks.

before.title: Rear Engine Mount Premature Failure
before.description: The Protege's rear engine mount (torque mount) fails prematurely, typically between 40,000-80,000 miles. The liquid-filled mount ruptures and collapses, allowing excessive engine movement during acceleration and braking. This causes a harsh clunk when shifting gears or a shuddering vibration at idle. The Protege5 and Mazdaspeed Protege are particularly prone due to their higher-torque engines.
before.solution: Replace the rear engine mount ($50-$100 for parts, 30-60 minutes labor). The mount is located at the rear of the engine below the intake manifold. OEM mounts last longer than cheap aftermarket. Mazdaspeed Protege owners often upgrade to polyurethane or solid mounts for reduced engine movement (at the cost of increased NVH). Check all mounts if the vehicle has over 100,000 miles.
symptoms: Harsh clunk when shifting into Drive or Reverse
Excessive vibration at idle in gear
Thump felt through floorboard on gear changes

before.title: Ignition switch may overheat and catch fire (Recall 15V674000)
before.description: Excessive grease applied to the contact points inside the ignition switch during production can carbonize over years of use and become electrically conductive, bridging the contacts. This reduces insulation inside the switch, allowing the contacts to overheat during continuous use. Owners may notice smoke from the steering column, a hot/melting key barrel, or a burning smell; in worst cases it can start a fire. Mazda recalled roughly 1.37 million U.S. vehicles across the 323/Protege (1990-1998), 626, MX-6, MX-3, 929, and MPV under NHTSA campaign 15V674000 (Mazda ref 8715J), announced October 2015 with the remedy beginning December 17, 2015.
before.solution: Have the ignition switch replaced. This was a free recall repair at Mazda dealers under 15V674000 (Mazda number 8715J); owners can verify open-recall status by VIN at NHTSA. On these age-of-vehicle cars the recall parts supply eventually dried up, so out-of-warranty replacement of the ignition switch by an independent shop is the practical fix today.

before.title: Structural rust: rocker panels, rear subframe/crossmember and strut towers
before.description: In salt-belt climates these Proteges rust from the underside up. Owners report perforated lower rocker panels at the seams, rusted-out floor sections (notably the rear passenger area), and - most importantly for safety - corrosion of the rear subframe/crossmember and rear strut towers. Mazda's factory primer/coating did not fully reach inside the rear crossmember, leaving bare steel exposed, so subframe rot can advance out of sight until it becomes a structural/safety concern (suspension mounting points weakening), sometimes reported as early as ~40,000 miles.
before.solution: Inspect the rear subframe, strut towers, floor pans, and rocker seams from underneath, probing suspected areas. Surface rust can be treated and undercoated; perforated or structurally compromised subframe/strut-tower/floor metal requires cut-and-weld repair with new sheet metal, and a severely rotted subframe should be replaced. Preventively, keep the underbody washed and apply cavity wax/undercoating.
symptoms: clunks or looseness from rear suspension mounts
